source.title: Symbolic Regression with a Learned Concept Library
source.authors: Arya Grayeli; Atharva Sehgal; Omar Costilla-Reyes; M. Cranmer; Swarat Chaudhuri

record.tranche_reason: The study uses symbolic regression on BigBench results to discover and evaluate a relationship between language-model training steps, in-context examples, and downstream scores. This is a different method from the original held-out pretraining-loss scaling measurements.
record.gate_note: The study does not report results on held-out pretraining cross-entropy, parameter/token/compute sweeps, or compute-optimal parameter-token allocation. Its BigBench score-prediction results bear on V6; the cited scaling-law results from other work are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The paper is mainly a symbolic-regression method paper. Its BigBench case study, though, fits scale-based equations (Chinchilla form in params and train_steps·batch_size, plus the discovered train_steps/#shots form) to downstream multiple-choice grade. It compares their held-out MSE with a constant-score baseline. That comparison bears on whether downstream performance is predictable from scale (V6). It uses a different method from the originals: equation fitting on pooled downstream scores, not pretraining-loss sweeps.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors say LaSR discovered a novel LLM scaling law whose BigBench MCQ-grade fit matches Chinchilla with fewer free parameters. They also concede that the constant score = E performs acceptably, that the results are preliminary, and that the discovered form generalizes poorly for even shot counts.
record.recipe_differences: Uses symbolic regression to discover an equation for BigBench MCQ grade from training steps and number of in-context examples, then fits and evaluates candidate equations on a train-validation split; it does not measure held-out pretraining loss or run a parameter/token/compute scaling sweep.
record.method_sensitivity: The discovered equation's behavior depends on the number of in-context examples: the authors note that even shot counts reverse the stated trend, while most training samples had odd shot counts.
record.problems: The LLM-scaling experiment is described as preliminary and uses one aggregate BigBench multiple-choice subset. The authors identify a generalization issue for even shot counts; the constant-score comparator also performs acceptably. The paper says whether observed trends generalize to higher-compute regimes remains to be seen.

untested.parts: No held-out pretraining loss or parameter/token/compute sweeps.
No extrapolation from small runs to larger ones. The BigBench validation split is random, not by scale.
No other modalities or training regimes.
Not tested: prediction from pretraining loss, extrapolation to larger models, and per-task predictability. Scores are pooled across all MCQ-grade tasks.
No comparison of fitted exponents or compute-optimal splits across setups.

missing.what: Search imposed a monotonic-increase constraint in training steps, so the discovered equation's direction with scale is assumed, not found.

record.verdict_notes: The record's untested note wrongly says the study doesn't test prediction from parameter scale. The Chinchilla comparator uses #params and train_steps·batch_size. The case study is a demonstration of the SR method, so the evidence for V6 is thin: one pooled subset, a random split, and no per-model or per-task breakdown.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining loss measurements or parameter, token, or compute sweeps.
No extrapolation from small pretraining runs to substantially larger runs.
No fixed-compute comparison or compute-optimal allocation between parameter count and token count.
No comparison of depth, width, or other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.
No tests of power-law scaling in other modalities or training regimes.

Tests prediction of BigBench multiple-choice grade from training steps and number of in-context examples on an aggregate subset; it does not test prediction from pretraining loss or parameter, token, or compute scale, nor across a broad set of downstream benchmarks.
Does not compare fitted exponents or compute-optimal splits across setups or fitting choices, or test whether pretraining-loss curves depart from power laws.

rows.subject: BigBench multiple-choice-grade subset (55 language models; aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Fit the LaSR-discovered score equation on the training set and evaluate predicted MCQ grade on a held-out validation set.

conditions.value: BigBench tasks with preferred metric 'Multiple choice grade' (53,812 samples)

rows.measure: Validation MSE for predicted MCQ grade
rows.note: The authors report performance competitive with Chinchilla, but describe the results as preliminary. They note that the equation's trend reverses for even numbers of shots, while most training samples had odd numbers.
rows.check: This row is the study's own discovered equation compared against others. Its baseline should be the constant-score fit (R4, MSE 0.09324), not 'not stated'. MSE falls to 0.03598, but residual error is large (RMSE about 0.19 on a 0–1 grade). The form also misbehaves for even shot counts. Monotonicity in training steps was imposed as a search constraint, so the trend is not discovered from data.

rows.subject: BigBench multiple-choice-grade subset (55 language models; aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Fit the Chinchilla equation's free parameters on the training set and evaluate predicted MCQ grade on a held-out validation set.

conditions.value: BigBench tasks with preferred metric 'Multiple choice grade' (53,812 samples)

rows.measure: Validation MSE for predicted MCQ grade
rows.note: Comparator equation evaluated on the same BigBench split.
rows.check: Baseline should be R4 (constant fit, 0.09324). The Chinchilla form in #params and train_steps·batch_size cuts held-out MSE to 0.03610. That is a clear gain, but residual error stays large and the authors call the constant baseline acceptable. The split is a random hold-out, not an extrapolation to larger models.

relationships.condition: Scale-based equations (Chinchilla, modified Chinchilla, discovered form) fitted to pooled BigBench MCQ grade, random held-out split
relationships.reason: Held-out MSE falls from 0.09324 (constant) to about 0.036 when scale variables are used (R1–R3 vs R4).
relationships.display_finding: Using scale variables reduces held-out mean squared error from 0.09324 for a constant baseline to about 0.036.

relationships.reason: Residual MSE stays large (RMSE about 0.19), and the authors call the constant fit acceptable and the results preliminary. The discovered form reverses for even shot counts (R1–R4).
relationships.display_finding: Residual RMSE remained around 0.19, a constant fit was considered acceptable, and the discovered relationship reversed for even numbers of shots.
